paragraphs: The paper studies monotone variational inequalities, a mathematical framework that can describe solutions to constrained convex optimization and convex-concave minimax problems. These problems include situations where competing objectives must reach an equilibrium. The authors propose fOGDA-VI, an algorithm that requires just one gradient or operator evaluation and one projection back onto the permitted set at each iteration.

Its main contribution is a convergence guarantee for the last iterate: the actual current solution estimate, rather than an average of previous estimates. Two measures of solution error, the restricted gap and natural residual, decrease at a rate of o(1/k). The paper also proves that the sequence of estimates converges to a solution.

Together, these results combine inexpensive iterations with strong theoretical progress guarantees under monotonicity. The authors describe them as the strongest reported guarantees for this setting. They evaluate the method on a two-player matrix game and report promising results for training generative adversarial networks; that application is presented as empirical evidence rather than an extension of the stated theoretical guarantees.
icml-2023-a-fast-optimistic-method-for-m.tldr: fOGDA-VI combines inexpensive updates with strong last-iterate convergence guarantees for monotone variational inequalities.

paragraphs: Online change point detection tracks a time series as observations arrive and looks for changes in its behavior. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that uses a Student-t process as its underlying time series model. It builds on an existing Gaussian process approach while seeking greater modeling flexibility and lower computational cost.

The Student-t process generalizes the Gaussian process, with a notable difference in how it represents uncertainty: its predictive variance explicitly depends on the observed training values. The authors combine this process with a dependent Student-t noise model. This coupled construction preserves analytical tractability, allowing the more flexible model to retain manageable mathematical calculations.

To reduce computational demands, the method approximates its kernel using a reduced-rank Hilbert space representation derived from Laplace-operator eigenfunctions. This provides a smaller representation for the calculations required by the process model. Experiments on real-world datasets report improvements in prediction and training time, supporting the combination of a more flexible uncertainty model with a computationally economical approximation.
icml-2023-bayesian-online-change-point-d.tldr: A reduced-rank Student-t process improves prediction and training time for Bayesian online change point detection in reported experiments.

paragraphs: BBF is a reinforcement learning agent designed to learn effectively from a limited amount of interaction. It uses a value-based approach, estimating how rewarding actions will be and using those estimates to guide behavior. The paper reports super-human performance on the Atari 100K benchmark, making sample efficiency central to its contribution.

A key ingredient is scaling up the neural networks used to estimate value. The authors pair this increase in network size with other design choices that make scaling work in a sample-efficient way. The contribution therefore concerns a combination of model capacity and training design, rather than a claim that increasing network size alone produces the reported result.

The paper extensively analyzes these design choices to provide insights for subsequent research. Its findings show that larger value-estimation networks can be part of an effective approach under the benchmark's interaction budget. The authors also discuss how research goals for sample-efficient learning on the Arcade Learning Environment might evolve in light of such performance.
icml-2023-bigger-better-faster-human-lev.tldr: BBF achieves super-human Atari 100K performance by combining larger value networks with design choices that support sample-efficient learning.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes learning with deep networks whose intermediate layers remain frozen while only the output layer is trained. The target is itself a random Gaussian network function. This extends the random features setting to deeper architectures and allows the authors to examine how architecture influences prediction error without training every layer.

For ridge regression, when the learner and target share their intermediate layers, the authors prove Gaussian universality of test error and derive a sharp asymptotic formula. Establishing this result involves a deterministic equivalent for traces of deep random feature covariance matrices: a predictable mathematical expression for quantities that otherwise depend on random matrices.

The paper then considers arbitrary convex losses and more general learner and target architectures. In this broader setting, Gaussian universality remains a conjecture supported by extensive numerical evidence, rather than a proved result. Closed-form layerwise covariance expressions support this analysis. Together, the results provide a way to investigate how network architecture interacts with implicit regularization and generalization.
icml-2023-deterministic-equivalent-and-e.tldr: The paper proves test-error universality for a specific deep random features setting and provides numerical evidence for a broader conjecture.

paragraphs: PRESTO learns a collection of specialized models while simultaneously deciding which data belong to each model. Its objective links the partitioning of the data to the performance of the model assigned to each partition. This makes clustering part of training itself, without assuming a particular generative process for the data.

The authors reformulate the task as parameter estimation combined with subset selection under a matroid span constraint. This mathematical structure lets them express the problem as constrained minimization of a monotone, approximately submodular set function. They then develop an algorithm that combines discrete partition decisions with continuous parameter updates and provides a bounded approximation guarantee.

The paper reports that PRESTO outperforms several alternative methods. It also applies the framework to resource-efficient deep learning, training smaller models tailored to separate data partitions. In that setting, PRESTO outperforms the compared partitioning, pruning, and knowledge-distillation approaches. Unlike those compared pruning and distillation approaches, its construction does not require beginning with a large teacher model.
icml-2023-discrete-continuous-optimizati.tldr: PRESTO jointly partitions data and trains specialized models, combining an approximation guarantee with reported gains in resource-efficient learning.

paragraphs: The paper asks when noise in stochastic gradient descent helps or harms generalization. It varies noise magnitude, training set size, and initialization scale. Initialization matters because it helps determine whether a network stays in a relatively fixed-feature, lazy regime or learns new features during training.

Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 produce phase diagrams showing that noise can improve or degrade performance depending on the training regime. Increasing noise and reducing initialization scale can both move a network away from lazy behavior, yet have opposite performance effects. The authors also find that the noise level at which training begins to change follows a power law in dataset size.

The authors connect these patterns to late training, when the network finishes fitting the data. They argue that noise requires larger informative weights and longer training to achieve that fit, with larger datasets creating related demands. Perceptron results support this interpretation where signal and noise can be measured directly. The scaling exponents also depend on how densely examples lie near the decision boundary.
icml-2023-dissecting-the-effects-of-sgd-.tldr: SGD noise can help or hurt depending on the training regime, with its effects linked to dataset size and late-stage fitting.

paragraphs: Covariate shift occurs when training and test inputs follow different distributions, while the relationship between inputs and labels remains the same. Standard correction methods weight either training examples or test examples using a ratio of those distributions. Such ratios can become very large, and mismatched distribution supports can make these approaches perform poorly.

This paper proposes weighting both sides through minimax risk classification. Instead of placing the whole adaptation burden on one set of weights, the method uses weights for both training and test samples. The authors develop procedures to obtain these weights that generalize kernel mean matching, connecting their approach to an established distribution-matching technique.

The theoretical contribution is a set of generalization bounds showing a substantially larger effective sample size than reweighting training examples alone. This concerns how much statistical information the weighted data provide, rather than an increase in the number of collected examples. Synthetic and empirical experiments also show improved classification performance, supporting the usefulness of double weighting within the covariate-shift setting.
icml-2023-double-weighting-for-covariate.tldr: Weighting both training and test samples improves covariate-shift adaptation, with stronger effective-sample-size bounds and better reported classification results.

paragraphs: Activity prediction models help estimate how chemicals behave in a particular task, but adapting them to new tasks typically requires training or fine-tuning. Scientific language models offer a possible route to prediction with little or no task-specific data, yet the paper identifies weak activity-prediction quality as a problem. CLAMP aims to connect chemical prediction with an understanding of task descriptions.

The architecture has separate modules for chemical inputs and natural-language inputs. It learns through a contrastive pretraining objective using large biochemical databases. This design lets the model use textual information describing a prediction task, supporting the goal of adapting at inference time rather than relying solely on task-specific parameter updates.

The authors report improved prediction on few-shot benchmarks and zero-shot drug-discovery problems. They attribute these gains to the modular architecture and the pretraining objective. The findings support combining specialized chemical and language representations for prediction when task data are scarce, with the reported evidence concerning predictive performance rather than downstream drug development outcomes.
icml-2023-enhancing-activity-prediction-.tldr: CLAMP combines chemical and language modules to improve activity prediction on few-shot and zero-shot drug-discovery tasks.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network involves updating a generator and a discriminator. A two time-scale update rule gives them different learning rates. This paper studies how batch size affects training when those learning rates are constant, distinguishing the number of update steps from the total stochastic gradient work needed.

The theoretical analysis shows that larger batches reduce the steps required to find stationary points of both loss functions. However, each larger batch involves more work per step. The authors prove that a critical batch size minimizes stochastic first-order oracle complexity, capturing the trade-off between taking fewer steps and processing more samples in each one.

The numerical study evaluates generated outputs using Fréchet inception distance. Larger batches require fewer steps to reach a low score, but oracle complexity rises once batch size exceeds the measured critical value. Those measured values are close to estimates derived from the theory. The results therefore support choosing batch size according to total training work rather than update count alone.
icml-2023-existence-and-estimation-of-cr.tldr: For GANs trained with constant-rate two time-scale updates, a critical batch size balances fewer updates against greater work per update.

paragraphs: Video-based facial expression recognition can be expensive when a model processes every frame. This paper proposes a sequential procedure that adjusts how many frames it examines within a short video fragment. Straightforward videos receive a lower processing frame rate, while more complex videos receive a higher one.

The central question is when the available frames provide sufficiently reliable evidence for a decision. The method uses the Benjamini-Hochberg multiple-testing procedure to control the false discovery rate when making this assessment. It maintains a single false-acceptance-rate hyperparameter, giving the adaptive selection process an explicit statistical criterion rather than relying only on a fixed frame budget.

The procedure can work with arbitrary neural networks used to extract facial features without retraining those networks. This makes frame selection an addition to an existing recognition system. Experiments on ABAW and EmotiW challenge datasets report speedups of 1.5 to 40 times relative to the evaluated full-frame, early-exit, and adaptive-selection techniques, showing the computational benefit of allocating more processing to difficult clips.
icml-2023-facial-expression-recognition-.tldr: Statistically guided frame selection speeds up facial expression recognition by processing fewer frames in easier videos.

paragraphs: Polar slice sampling is a Markov chain method for approximately drawing samples from a probability distribution. Its behavior with increasing dimension has attractive theoretical properties, but implementing it efficiently is difficult. This paper develops a family of practical samplers inspired by that method, aiming to make its underlying approach computationally usable.

The key change is to update direction and radius separately. A point can be described by the direction it faces from an origin and its distance from that origin; separating those components changes how each sampling step is performed. The resulting methods mimic polar slice sampling while permitting efficient implementation.

Numerical experiments across several settings indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms elliptical slice sampling and hit-and-run uniform slice sampling, the two closely related methods considered. The authors also prove that their methods are well-defined and converge under suitable assumptions on the target distribution. These guarantees support the construction, while the comparative performance claim rests on the reported experiments.
icml-2023-gibbsian-polar-slice-sampling-.tldr: Updating direction and radius separately makes polar-inspired slice sampling practical, with conditional convergence guarantees and favorable numerical results.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what a graph neural network can learn from connections alone. Its analysis considers graph-generation processes controlled by hidden node features that contain all information about graph structure. One example is a nearest-neighbor graph formed from those features, where connections reflect relationships among underlying node descriptions.

Within this framework, the authors show that GNNs can recover hidden features even when the input includes no node features or indirect hints about them. The recovered features can then support downstream tasks. The result gives a theoretical account of how connectivity itself can carry usable feature information, beyond whatever explicit attributes accompany a graph.

The authors construct a GNN architecture informed by the analysis and experimentally demonstrate accurate hidden-feature recovery. Together, the theory and experiments support a strong expressive capability for the considered graph-generation setting. The scope matters: the recovery result concerns graphs whose structure is controlled by the specified hidden-feature process, rather than an unrestricted assertion about every possible graph.
icml-2023-graph-neural-networks-can-reco.tldr: For the studied latent-feature graph-generation setting, GNNs can recover hidden node features from connectivity alone.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks to infer rewards from behavior. This paper studies that problem when the decision process also includes constraints, motivated by the need to learn appropriate objectives while accounting for safety. It develops a convex-analytic framework covering constrained Markov decision processes and a broader class of regularization choices.

A central issue is identifiability: how precisely behavior determines the underlying reward. The authors show that an existing identification result, which permits ambiguity through potential shaping, follows from entropy regularization. That result may cease to hold with other regularizers or safety constraints. Consequently, conclusions about reward recovery depend on how the learning problem is formulated.

The paper also shows that guaranteeing generalization to new transition laws and constraints requires identifying the true reward up to an additive constant. This is a more demanding recovery target than allowing potential-shaping ambiguity. A finite-sample guarantee bounds the suboptimality associated with learned rewards, and gridworld experiments validate the analysis. The work connects the precision of reward recovery to its ability to transfer.
icml-2023-identifiability-and-generaliza.tldr: Constraints and regularization change which rewards can be identified, and guaranteed transfer requires recovering the true reward up to a constant.

paragraphs: In incentivized bandit exploration, an algorithm recommends actions to people whose interests must be respected. Recommendations are required to be Bayesian incentive compatible, so exploration must fit with the users' incentives under the model. The challenge is to gather useful information while maintaining that compatibility.

Previous results established that Thompson sampling becomes incentive compatible after sufficient initial data collection for independent arms, with a subsequent extension to combinatorial semibandits. This paper proves an analogous result for linear bandits. In its analysis, a natural convexity condition replaces the earlier independence assumption on the prior, extending the circumstances in which this exploration strategy can be justified.

The extension opens the possibility of efficient, regret-optimal incentivized exploration in high-dimensional action spaces. The abstract presents that prospect as an implication of the result, rather than an unconditional guarantee for all such spaces. The paper also improves the sample complexity of initial data collection in the semibandit setting, reducing the preparation needed before switching to Thompson sampling.
icml-2023-incentivizing-exploration-with.tldr: The paper extends incentive-compatible Thompson sampling to linear bandits under a convexity condition and improves semibandit initialization sample complexity.

paragraphs: The paper proposes learning informative priors for neural networks to improve generalization and uncertainty estimation. Its core idea is to reuse scalable, structured posterior distributions as priors. This carries forward a probabilistic representation of what a model has learned, providing a Bayesian counterpart to the role played by pretrained models.

The approach supports expressive representations at large scale and produces non-vacuous generalization bounds. These are bounds that remain informative rather than becoming too loose to say anything useful. Two technical components make this possible: computations involving sums of Kronecker products, and tractable training objectives whose derivation and optimization improve the resulting bounds.

The authors also extend the method to continual learning, where information learned previously can inform subsequent learning. Empirical evaluations report benefits for both uncertainty estimation and generalization. The contribution therefore combines a reusable probabilistic representation with mathematical guarantees, rather than treating predictive accuracy and uncertainty as entirely separate goals.
icml-2023-learning-expressive-priors-for.tldr: Structured neural-network posteriors become expressive learned priors, supporting improved uncertainty estimation, generalization, and informative theoretical bounds.

paragraphs: VC-INR compresses data by treating each item as a function represented by an implicit neural network. Its aim is to use a common compression method across different kinds of data. Rather than assigning an entirely separate network to every item, it specializes a shared network through compact latent representations.

Those latent representations are mapped nonlinearly into soft gates that select subnetworks. This connects compact coding with sparsity: the code determines which parts of the shared representation serve a particular item. After learning these codes, the method applies neural compression directly in their shared space, optimizing the trade-off between storage rate and reconstruction distortion.

The authors report better performance at equal representational capacity before quantization, along with improvements over earlier INR quantization schemes. Experiments span images, climate data, 3D shapes and scenes, audio, and video without modality-specific inductive biases. The reported comparisons include outperforming JPEG 2000, MP3, and AVC/HEVC on their respective modalities, demonstrating the breadth of the approach in the tested settings.
icml-2023-modality-agnostic-variational-.tldr: VC-INR uses compact codes to specialize and compress shared neural representations across diverse data modalities.

paragraphs: Markov jump processes describe systems that switch states randomly in continuous time. Although widely used in natural and social sciences, inferring their hidden behavior from observations is difficult. This paper proposes a variational inference method as an alternative to approaches based on Monte Carlo sampling or expectation maximization.

The method uses neural ordinary differential equations to learn continuous-time representations of observed data, and it can be trained through back-propagation. Those representations approximate the initial state distribution and time-dependent transition rates of the posterior process. In other words, they describe plausible process behavior after taking the observations into account.

The prior process has time-independent transition rates, which are trained through a procedure analogous to generative adversarial network training. This separates how the baseline process is learned from how observations shape the posterior. The authors test the approach using synthetic processes with known ground truth, experimental ion-channel switching data, and molecular dynamics simulations, examining its use across controlled and scientific examples.
icml-2023-neural-markov-jump-processes-4.tldr: Neural ordinary differential equations enable a back-propagation-trained variational inference method for continuous-time Markov jump processes.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning under an average-reward objective, which evaluates sustained reward rather than discounting rewards farther into the future. It focuses especially on off-policy actor-critic learning, where the policy being improved can differ from the one that produced the training experience. The authors identify this combination as relatively underexplored.

They derive deterministic policy-gradient theorems for both on-policy and off-policy average-reward learning. These results underpin ARO-DDPG, an off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithm. The paper also provides asymptotic convergence analysis using an ordinary-differential-equation method, connecting the learning updates to a mathematical account of their long-run behavior.

A separate finite-time analysis addresses the stochastic approximation scheme with a linear function approximator. It reports an epsilon-optimal stationary policy with sample complexity Ω(epsilon^−2.5); this statement specifically concerns that linear setting. Experiments in MuJoCo-based environments show better average-reward performance than the compared state-of-the-art on-policy average-reward actor-critic methods, providing empirical support for the proposed off-policy algorithm.
icml-2023-off-policy-average-reward-acto.tldr: ARO-DDPG brings deterministic off-policy actor-critic learning to average reward, supported by gradient theorems, convergence analysis, and MuJoCo results.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning often requires extensive trial and error. Model-based methods seek to use experience more efficiently by learning an environment model and planning with it. This paper develops PSDRL, a scalable approximation to posterior sampling for reinforcement learning that retains this model-based structure.

PSDRL combines uncertainty quantification over latent state-space models with an incremental planning algorithm based on value-function approximation. The latent models provide a representation of environment dynamics, while uncertainty quantification captures uncertainty about those models. The tailored planner makes that model information usable for decision-making at the scale targeted by deep reinforcement learning.

Experiments on Atari show that PSDRL significantly outperforms earlier state-of-the-art attempts to scale posterior sampling. It is also competitive with a state-of-the-art model-based method in both sample efficiency and computational efficiency. These findings support the feasibility of combining posterior-sampling ideas with deep models and practical planning, rather than relying on the favorable results previously established in tabular settings alone.
icml-2023-posterior-sampling-for-deep-re.tldr: PSDRL scales model-based posterior sampling through latent-model uncertainty estimates and incremental planning, with strong Atari efficiency results.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether self-distillation gains can arise from training dynamics themselves. To isolate that possibility, it uses teachers at random initialization rather than trained teachers. Students trained against these random teachers show substantially better probing accuracy, indicating that useful representations can emerge even without a knowledgeable teacher.

The learned representations depend on the data and transfer between tasks, but deteriorate strongly when training uses random inputs. The resulting student checkpoints also contain sparse subnetworks described as lottery tickets and sit near the borders of linear basins in the supervised loss landscape. Feature learning becomes stronger when the student starts close to the teacher.

These observations support the possibility that implicit regularization in gradient dynamics can make self-distillation work without transferring a trained teacher's dark knowledge. They also show that feature learning can occur without data augmentation and suggest that early supervised-training dynamics need not always require labels. These are demonstrations of what can happen in the studied setting, rather than universal requirements for successful representation learning.
icml-2023-random-teachers-are-good-teach.tldr: Students trained against randomly initialized teachers can learn useful transferable features, revealing a role for training dynamics in self-distillation.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should receive labels, making selective use of labeling effort. Many deep-learning approaches assume they can inspect the entire dataset before making those choices. This paper addresses a streaming setting, where examples arrive over time and decisions about requesting labels must be made as they are encountered.

The proposed algorithm, VeSSAL, performs batch active learning by sampling groups of incoming points. It balances uncertainty with diversity: the selection considers both where the model is uncertain and how varied the queried examples are. The method targets a desired query rate without requiring hand-tuned hyperparameters to manage this trade-off.

This changes the information-access requirements of deep active learning. Selection no longer depends on having an offline view of all examples in advance, which makes the approach relevant to human-computer interaction and large datasets spread across separate pieces. The paper's stated contribution is an algorithm suited to these streaming circumstances, with label selection organized around arrival-time decisions and a chosen query rate.
icml-2023-streaming-active-learning-with.tldr: VeSSAL selects examples for labeling as they arrive, balancing uncertainty and diversity while matching a desired query rate.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models must balance image quality with generation speed. The paper starts from the observation that leading iterative models require repeated evaluations to produce an image, whereas a GAN can generate one in a single forward pass. StyleGAN-T aims to make that speed advantage useful while improving GAN performance on large-scale text-conditioned generation.

The model addresses several requirements together: sufficient capacity, stable training on diverse data, strong correspondence between images and text, and control over the trade-off between variation and text alignment. That last requirement matters because the system must accommodate both producing varied outputs and adhering closely to a supplied description.

The authors report substantial improvements over previous GANs. They also report better sample quality and speed than distilled diffusion models, identified as the previous leading approach for fast text-to-image synthesis. The stated comparison establishes progress within fast generation, rather than a claim of superiority over every text-to-image model. The work positions GAN design as a viable route to better quality at low generation cost.
icml-2023-stylegan-t-unlocking-the-power.tldr: StyleGAN-T improves fast text-to-image generation, outperforming the compared distilled diffusion models in both sample quality and speed.

paragraphs: Children acquire an intuitive understanding of physical processes through developmental stages. This paper asks whether deep generative neural networks develop physical knowledge along similar learning trajectories. The comparison concerns how abilities emerge over learning, rather than only whether a trained model eventually predicts a physical process accurately.

The authors outline an approach for examining two hypotheses about human development: stochastic optimization and increasing complexity. Physical understanding provides the testbed for comparing the models' learning paths with developmental patterns documented in earlier empirical research. This makes the order and progression of learned abilities central to the evaluation.

The models accurately predict several physical processes, but their learning trajectories under both hypotheses fail to match those of children. The finding separates successful prediction from a successful account of development: reaching useful behavior does not by itself reproduce the path children take. For the models and hypotheses examined, predictive competence therefore offers only part of what would be needed to explain the acquisition of human physical knowledge.
icml-2023-the-acquisition-of-physical-kn.tldr: The studied generative networks predict physical processes accurately but do not acquire those abilities along children's developmental trajectories.

paragraphs: Functional data are naturally viewed as functions rather than fixed arrays of measurements. Neural operators model relationships between such functions, enabling representations that do not depend on a particular discretization grid. This paper introduces VANO, a general strategy for turning a broad class of operator-learning architectures into variational autoencoders.

VANO encodes an input function as a distribution in latent space. It then samples from that distribution and decodes the sample to reconstruct the function. The authors provide a rigorous formulation of the variational training objective in function spaces, giving this familiar encoding-and-reconstruction pattern a mathematical foundation suited to functional data.

The evaluation spans different architectures and model setups. It begins with a Gaussian random field, where the learned behavior can be tracked analytically, then moves to phase separation in Cahn-Hilliard systems and satellite measurements of Earth-surface deformation. These tests examine the framework from a mathematically interpretable example through more demanding physical and real-world data, illustrating the range of functional modeling problems it targets.
icml-2023-variational-autoencoding-neura.tldr: VANO gives neural operators a variational autoencoder formulation for learning probabilistic representations of functional data.

paragraphs: Language models answering subjective questions reflect viewpoints that may differ from those of their users. This paper develops a quantitative way to examine those differences using public opinion polls. Its dataset, OpinionQA, compares model responses with opinions from 60 US demographic groups across subjects ranging from abortion to automation.

The authors find substantial misalignment across topics between the evaluated models and these demographic groups. They contextualize its size by comparing it with the Democrat-Republican divide on climate change. Explicitly steering models toward particular demographic groups does not eliminate the mismatch, showing that such instructions do not necessarily make responses representative of the requested population.

The analysis also confirms left-leaning tendencies in some models tuned with human feedback and identifies poorly represented groups, including people aged 65 and older and widowed individuals. These findings concern the views expressed in model responses. They make demographic representation measurable and show why a model's answers to subjective questions should not automatically be treated as reflecting its users' opinions.
icml-2023-whose-opinions-do-language-mod.tldr: OpinionQA finds substantial gaps between language-model responses and US demographic opinions, even when models are prompted to represent specific groups.
